item.title: Democrats have reached a détente in their internal war. Will it last?
item.description: A new POLITICO Poll finds that moderates and progressives feel more unified. But cracks remain over how to deliver for voters and 2028.

media:content.media:credit: Illustration by Anna Wiederkehr/POLITICO (source images via Getty)
media:content.media:title: TPP: Dem Alignment

item.dc:creator: By Lisa Kashinsky
item.content:encoded:
Democrats’ long-warring ideological factions have reached a détente, new POLITICO Poll data shows. It may not last.

Half of progressives and moderates now say the party is “somewhat” or “much more” unified since the election, according to the latest survey, conducted last weekend by PF Global. And everyone agrees on what the Democratic-led Congress needs to do first, above anything else: bring down the cost of living.

The size and sweep of Democrats’ midterms romp appears to have temporarily quelled the electability questions that fueled the long-running standoff between the party’s factions. Progressives flipped House districts and snagged Senate seats on plainly purple turf. Many moderate candidates flipped deep-red territory for the first time in decades. Put together, Democrats are now headed for their biggest House majority of the century.

“We’ve got this great big-tent party that’s coming into Congress, and I think that’s what people want,” said Pete Giangreco, a veteran Democratic strategist who worked across House, Senate and gubernatorial races this past cycle. “They don’t want these ideological divisions”

Today, two out of three Democratic midterm voters believe that progressives make their party stronger — considerably higher than the 41% who said so before Election Day, according to polls taken before and after the midterms. Among self-described moderate Democrats, that belief has risen 26 points, from 33% to 59%. Among progressives, it’s risen from 58% to 74%.

“If people are spending more time going after other Democrats instead of figuring out how to work together as a team, then I'm not sure that they've got the right priorities,” moderate Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) told POLITICO.

But it’s not clear how long the unity will last.

The polling reveals cracks are already starting to reemerge within Democrats’ coalition, foreshadowing potential intraparty fights to come on Capitol Hill and beyond into 2028. Democrats agree on the broad strokes of their priorities, but they diverge on the scope of lawmakers’ approach and the kind of presidential nominee they’d like to see.

“Democrats, they don’t need to be getting too big-headed about this quote-unquote blue wave or blue tsunami,” said incoming Arizona 6th District Rep. JoAnna Mendoza. “What they need to focus on is making sure that we’re bringing people relief and that we’re taking action because that’s what people need right now.”

The poll bears out two of Democrats’ near-universal takeaways from last Tuesday that are already shaping the shadow 2028 presidential primary: Voters want to elect fighters — and they want them to cut down high costs.

The overwhelming majority of Democratic midterm voters — 78% — say bringing down the cost of living should be Democrats’ top focus as they come into control of Congress next year. Nearly as many, 71%, of Americans said the same.

But Democratic voters internally disagree on approach. The POLITICO Poll data shows 47% of the party’s midterm voters prefer the next Congress’ agenda be set by Democrats who want major systemic reforms and government intervention to reduce inequality, compared to 39% who prefer Democrats who want pragmatic and targeted economic solutions.

A majority of progressives, 57%, choose systemic reform. Moderates, meanwhile, are split between systemic reform (43%) and targeted economic solutions (44%)

Those splits are poised to spill onto the presidential campaign trail. Even as voters broadly agree on wanting a “fighter” candidate, half of progressives still think someone with their ideology would be among the most electable in 2028, while just over a third of moderates, 36%, say someone in their lane has the best shot.

Several possible White House aspirants are trying to push a public truce, arguing that factional infighting needs to take a backseat for now.

"I don't think any voters think about it that way," Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro told reporters when asked by POLITICO whether there was a progressive or moderate takeaway from the midterms at Crooked Media's post-election conference in D.C. "People want to see the results of their government because whether you voted for Trump or Harris in the last election, your prices are still too damn high."

Progressive Rep. Ro Khanna, in a post-election interview, said “we had electability across the board” in the midterms and that the question heading into 2028 is “who has the best vision for America.”

Lauren Fedor contributed to this report.

item.title: Meet the 27-year-old behind the protein ad that helped flip Mississippi
item.description: One of this cycle’s biggest viral hits offers Democrats a potential blueprint as they think about competing in the South — and their digital strategy ahead of 2028.

media:content.media:title: Ryan Sayles, left, and Scott Colom.

item.dc:creator: By Erin Doherty
item.content:encoded:
You know you’ve made a good ad when it’s outperforming an endorsement video from Barack Obama.

Ryan Sayles, a 27-year-old Mississippi content creator, is behind arguably the best political spot of the election cycle: Democrat Scott Colom’s viral “pick another protein” ad against GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

You’ve probably seen it by now. The ad featured Mississippi voters’ blunt reactions to Hyde-Smith’s suggestion that people struggling with rising beef prices choose from other protein options.

“Pick another protein? Shiiii-, I’d rather pick another senator instead.”

“Pick another protein? She done lost her damn mind. I’d rather pick another senator.”

Sayles was at his nephew’s football game when he realized something extraordinary was happening.

“I was looking at the first numbers when it first dropped, and I was like, ‘Oh, this is about to be a really good video,’” he told POLITICO after Colom’s historic Senate race victory in the longtime Republican stronghold. “We had the Obama endorsement the day before, so that was our biggest video. It was like, ‘Dang, we ain’t ever gonna top that.’”

“And then this ad came, and we posted it, and it outperformed anything we ever did,” Sayles said.

The 30-second spot quickly became the talk of Mississippi and Washington, helping fuel Colom’s longshot campaign to unseat Hyde-Smith and become the first Black senator from the state since Reconstruction. And, it’s given Democrats across the country another blueprint for how to break through online ahead of a critical 2028 presidential race, as the party continues to rethink its strategy.

With the ad — and Colom’s win — Sayles has gone from a newcomer who stumbled into campaigning almost by accident to a name to watch in Democratic digital politics, as the party looks for fresh ways to reach voters ahead of 2028.

“[Sayles] should be considered the breakout-star of this cycle,” Colom wrote in a post on X about the viral ad earlier this month. “He’s going to be a giant in the media consultant game. He did GAME CHANGING work with SO little.”

In an interview with POLITICO, Sayles described how his lack of prior political experience shaped his approach to creating the ad and why he thinks Democrats should listen more closely to the voters they’re trying to reach. He also discussed the unexpected attention he’s received since the ad — and why he hopes Colom’s victory will serve as a wake-up call for the party to invest in the South.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

How did you get involved with the Colom campaign? 

I did a lot of freelance videography and photography, and they really just needed a photographer for one event they were doing back in October. And I came and did video and pictures for him, and they kept me around.

They were like, "Yeah, we need to work with him,” and then from then on, I never left.

Take me behind the scenes of creating the protein ad. How did it come together? 

Scott and his brother, Andrew, along with [the] campaign manager Gerard, they all plotted the script together, and so they presented it to me.

We filmed it, and I directed and made sure it [felt] like Mississippi. I guess I made it more Mississippi than what it was at the beginning.

You know, [I] just added the entertainment or funny pieces of it, like emphasizing the way he said the words and stuff like that. And then I shot it, edited it, and added the music to it.

I sat there and edited for like five hours. I've heard that man say “shit” a million times.

Did you think it was going to go this viral? 

I had high hopes for it, but I just didn't know what it could do.

A lot of our content was getting around Mississippi, but it wasn't getting around the country. Mississippians knew about Scott Colom’s content and what he was doing, but it wasn't nationwide — and I think that ad really put a national focus on what was brewing in Mississippi.

Why do you think this particular ad took off so much and felt so natural? 

I think the reason it did well nationally is because I think a lot of people are fed up.

A lot of times we don't express the way we feel, we hold it in, but I think this ad was an expression that people felt all around the country, that we just had the guts to put it out there.

For Mississippi, of course it resonated because that's something we say down here. People say “shiiiit” all the time — like you know, that's the normal conversation.

I think the best thing about the ad was it was centering people, centering voters ... You know, Scott was in the ad for about five seconds, but then that was the biggest ad of the cycle. I think it was just a lesson that people matter way more than politics.

Did anybody worry the ad went too far? Do you think Democrats are sometimes too cautious? 

I think the dope part is, we didn't run that ad by anybody. … We didn’t go around getting OK’s from anybody ... we just put it out. But also … I've never worked on a campaign, and I think that I didn't have a sense of what Dems normally did. You know what I mean?

We just did what we liked, and that was one of the big things Scott always talked about. “Man, if we are good with the content, we are good.”

Scott is the best person I could’ve been in this situation with. He has been such a great person. He’s so creative, and he has allowed me to shine in ways that I just can’t believe.

Did you hear from people in the Democratic Party after the ad came out?

Like I said, this is my first campaign, so this is all a blur right now, honestly. But I would say that I've gotten messages, a lot of messages. I don't know who all those messages are tied to at this point, but I have gotten a lot of messages and people saying, “You did great work, we should talk.”

I'm just happy. Mississippi is, we have hope again, man, that's the biggest thing. You know, this is my state.

What could the Democratic Party learn from the Colom campaign’s digital strategy? 

I want to shout out my digital director. Lacy Nelson was the digital director, and she really helped turn things around when it came to just our distribution being able to put stuff out, because at first I was posting, taking pictures, filming, editing, doing everything by myself, and it was the worst headache.

You gotta put your feet on the ground, you gotta understand the area in which you are working to try to get voters, and you gotta let them know that you see them and make them feel seen.

You have to understand what resonates with people. People in Mississippi are not going to care about the things that somebody who lives in New York City cares about, it's going to be different. And that messaging needs to be different. You can't give Mississippi a New York message.

Not that I'm an expert — like I said, this is my first campaign — but I think people should really focus on what that region is listening to.

What does Colom’s victory mean for Democrats’ opportunities across the South? 

For a long time we’ve looked at it as impossible. And with very little resources, we showed that if you really get out and you do the work, you talk to people, you meet voters where they are, it is possible.

Mississippi is one of the hardest places that could have happened. When you look at the investment and you look at what other places have received for that type of thing, it shows that the opportunity was always in Mississippi. … We just needed the investment, and I think that over the years, so many organizations have done the work to get us to this point, and we just seized the opportunity.

There's real opportunity in the South. You just gotta invest.

item.title: 2028 Dems: Don’t label me
item.description: Democrats with eyes on the White House are hoping to push the party past its long-running ideological war.

media:content.media:title: Maryland Governor Wes Moore (left) talks with Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro during an event with governors from across the country in the East Room of the White House on February 23, 2024 in Washington, D.C.

item.dc:creator: By Lisa Kashinsky
item.content:encoded:
Democrats’ midterms sweep didn’t solve their ideological civil war — but a number of the party’s potential presidential contenders hope it lets them call a truce.

In the days since Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories, several likely White House aspirants have argued that their party’s factional feuding needs to take a backseat heading into 2028.

“What was clear, no matter where you go, [is that] people are frustrated,” Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro told reporters last weekend at Crooked Media’s post-election conference. “They're not thinking about whether this is about left or middle or right. They're thinking about how to get problems solved.”

“I don't know if the takeaway should be what ideology that people wanted. I think people want results,” Maryland Gov. Wes Moore said at the same event.

Democrats’ midterm tidal wave was powered more by voters’ anger at high costs and the Trump administration than by any one ideology. Candidates won tough races by positioning themselves not as progressives or moderates but as anti-Washington populists and pragmatists — some of them even scoring dual endorsements from both the moderate Blue Dog Democrats and progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.).

“If you see … an elected leader spending valuable time duking it out on whose team won, moderate or progressive, they are missing the actual message of this election,” Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, a moderate who campaigned hard for progressive Abdul El-Sayed, told POLITICO. “It’s about people who are wanting to work together as a team on issues like the American dream in the middle class.”Many of the party’s rising stars embraced an ethos like Shapiro’s “get stuff done” and, like Slotkin, called to reject progressive-versus-moderate politics in favor of combative candidates.

“It helps take away the most annoying question that has split our party, and that is the question of electability,” progressive Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) said in an interview last week. “It turns out that progressives were electable, and centrists were electable. The moderates were electable, and people who were affiliated with the DSA were electable.”

Now, as they pivot into 2028, Democrats are broadly seizing on last week’s results as license to avoid traditional labels as they look to appeal as widely as possible to voters more interested in easing the pinch in their pocketbooks than the political philosophy to which their leaders subscribe. Interviews and conversations with more than a dozen potential Democratic presidential candidates, advisers and operatives reveal that rhetorical shift is as much a rejection of the ideological litmus tests that dominated the 2020 primary as it is a calibration toward the dynamics that will drive the 2028 contest.

“We all lived through the purity tests,” said Adrienne Elrod, a Democratic strategist who advised Joe Biden in 2020, Kamala Harris in 2024 and Hillary Clinton’s 2016 run. “What people are now yearning for is authenticity. And they want a fighter and someone who can deliver more than someone who perfectly aligns with them ideologically.”

There are tells in the flurry of postelection memos from potential presidential contenders. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s team positioned her not as a progressive firebrand but as “one of the most effective voices in the country for America’s working class.” Teams behind Moore and Shapiro pushed messages of “common-sense governance” and “delivering results.”

“There has been a reckoning in the Democratic Party, and people in all lanes frankly have come to realize the government in Washington has not delivered for working-class people and they need to,” said Jeff Weaver, a Khanna adviser who managed Sanders’ 2016 presidential campaign.

Or, as one adviser to a potential candidate said: Voters “do not live in the binaries that a lot of political operatives do.”

While last Tuesday’s wave swept Democrats of all stripes into office, it also created openings for each wing of the party to argue that its vision is the way forward. That all but guarantees more proxy battles to come as the party moves from running a raft of candidates across diverse districts to selecting just one to try and win the White House.

The left has seized on strong performances by unabashedly progressive candidates to push Khanna and Ocasio-Cortez to run for president and Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) to challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) for Senate majority leader.

Ravi Mangla, a spokesperson for the Working Families Party, said it’s “undeniable the populist candidates … can win in swing states that are going to be critical in 2028” — and the left lane is “wide open.”

But the centrist group Welcome argued in a new memo shared first with POLITICO that there’s a clear pathway for candidates willing to embrace a more moderate posture.

“In a very large field, you need a base to get you to 15, 20, 25 percent. And it’s very clear in the data you can get there with voters in the middle — center-left voters,” said Welcome co-founder Liam Kerr.

And even as he called for a primary that would battle test a diverse set of ideological views, Khanna, who co-chaired Sanders’ 2020 campaign, leaned into his liberal bona fides: “It would be an honor to be called a Bernie Sanders Democrat; I embrace being a New Deal Democrat with pride.”

“Obviously, I'm a progressive Democrat. I believe that the progressive vision is the best vision. But there should be someone who’s in the center or center-left. Then they can argue for their vision,” Khanna said. “And then it’s for the American people and the primary to decide.”

item.title: Mississippi elects Democrat Scott Colom to Senate in massive upset
item.description: Colom's win is a boost to the Democratic Party as it seeks to gain a larger foothold in the South.

media:content.media:title: Scott Colom speaks during a news conference at the Hinds County Sheriff's Office in Jackson, Mississippi, on Nov. 10, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Jason Beeferman
item.content:encoded:
Mississippi voted blue, in a shock win for Democrats.

Democrat Scott Colom ousted Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a state that went for President Donald Trump by 23 points in 2024. He will be the first Black senator elected in Mississippi since the Reconstruction era — and the first Democrat from the state headed to the Senate in 44 years.

Colom, a Democratic district attorney, ran a scrappy campaign that saw some national money and resources in the final stretch of the race.

Hyde-Smith was appointed to the Senate in 2018 and had since won election to the seat twice, but she faced attacks from Colom that she was out of touch and indifferent to rising grocery and gas prices during Trump’s second term.

National Democratic groups hadn't paid much attention to the Mississippi Senate race until an October surge of excitement for Colom drew late spending and attention.

Colom's win is a boost to the Democratic Party as it seeks to gain a larger foothold in the South and improve their standing with Black voters. It’s also a major vindication for Colom and other Southern Democrats who argued Mississippi had been neglected for far too long.

item.title: ‘Draft Marco’ effort grows on Capitol Hill after midterms bloodbath
item.description: More and more Republicans see a wide open 2028 presidential race — and are eyeing Marco Rubio.

media:content.media:credit: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call via Getty Images
media:content.media:title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio talks to Rep. María Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) during a House Foreign Affairs Committee hearing on June 3, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Meredith Lee Hill and Mia McCarthy
item.dc:contributor: By Meredith Lee Hill and Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
A growing number of Republicans on Capitol Hill want to draft Marco Rubio for a 2028 presidential bid as they grapple with their midterms wipeout — and look beyond Vice President JD Vance.

The generational losses are sparking new discussions among Hill Republicans about who should lead the party. Many argue the race to carry the mantle is now wide open — including a faction who view Rubio as a better fit, given that voters may continue to tie Vance to the president’s unpopularity, interviews with roughly two dozen GOP lawmakers reveal.

“I hope he runs. I think he's the best person to communicate, to unify,” Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-Ind.) said of Rubio in an interview.

“I think he's the most talented Republican by far,” Stutzman said when asked about why he supported the secretary of State over Vance. “We're going to have to continue to re-message, put some new faces up.” The vice president still has his supporters. And he got a boost Tuesday by fellow Ohio Republican Jim Jordan being elected as the incoming House minority leader.

But the election wipeout “certainly makes it harder for Vance,” said one GOP senator, who like others in this article, was granted anonymity to speak candidly.

“I think Rubio is our best hope to lead Republicans out of this wilderness, and I hope he makes his break from Trump and JD early next year,” said one House Republican in the wake of the election.

The openness toward Rubio — or any other candidate that’s not Vance — is a complication for the vice president, who was picked by Trump for the role that’s next in line to the presidency. Now, Vance has to grapple with being closely associated with an agenda that even GOP lawmakers argue voters harshly rebuked last week.

Several lawmakers said they’ve spoken to people close to Rubio who have suggested he isn’t interested in pursuing a 2028 bid, even after Tuesday’s results. Rubio himself this week has stood by Trump’s decision to go to war against Iran and told reporters Monday he was “just not going to talk about 2028 anymore.”

A person close to Rubio said the secretary of State is the only person who knows what he will do regarding a presidential bid. Right now, he’s “fully focused on doing his many jobs and isn’t thinking about 2028.”

But some Hill Republicans aren’t giving up hope.

“I’m a big supporter of Marco Rubio, and I’m very excited about the potential of his candidacy,” said Florida Rep. Mike Haridopolos, who has known the secretary of State for nearly three decades. “No question he’s ready to be president if he chooses to pursue the office.”

“Some of us are still hoping we can draft Marco,” said another GOP senator.

A State Department spokesperson declined to comment. Vance’s office didn’t respond to a request for comment.

In reaction to Stutzman’s comments, a Vance ally argued that Stutzman has been one of the biggest supporters within the GOP of amnesty for unauthorized immigrants for over a decade — and that he was likely never going to support Vance, who is extremely hawkish on border security.

Vance, for his part, has tried to distance himself from the unpopular Iran war, blaming it for the party’s losses in the immediate aftermath of the midterm election. His allies argue that the vice president would’ve always faced some internal opposition, like Trump did within the GOP ahead of the 2016 election.

However, as the Rubio talk swirls, even some of Trump’s top MAGA allies on Capitol Hill are unwilling to publicly declare Vance the presumptive GOP nominee for 2028. “Can I skip this one?” one House GOP hardliner said. “Not wading into 2028 yet.” Some Republican senators also declined to back Vance just yet, citing their own reelections.

GOP Rep. and Sen.-elect Barry Moore of Alabama said he thought Vance would certainly “have a shot” at the presidency in 2028. Moore was the first member of Congress to back Trump for the 2016 race.

But Moore for now is leaving his endorsement up in the air: “We got a great bench," he said. "Whoever steps up, we'll be happy to support.”

Rubio’s supporters say that he’s not as closely associated with the 2026 GOP wipeout as Vance, but he could face his own obstacles. Rubio, unlike Vance, has continued to show strong support for the war in Iran, a conflict he’s tied to as the country’s top diplomat. Some GOP lawmakers have also grown frustrated with the amount of information the Trump administration, including Rubio at times, has been willing to share about the ongoing conflict.

Rubio also has his failed 2016 presidential run to contend with, including an infamous debate performance where he awkwardly repeated the same rehearsed line multiple times.

One thing is clear, the 2028 presidential race is now wide open, many Hill Republicans argue as they process Tuesday’s results. And other potential candidates only appear encouraged after the midterms wipeout.

Several Hill Republicans believe outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, who has been one of the most outspoken Republicans urging a course correction after the midterms bloodbath, will get in the race as well. Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) this week also didn’t rule out a presidential bid. Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) also appears likely to run.

“I think everybody reserves the right to adjust. You know, learn from this,” GOP Rep. and incoming Oklahoma Sen. Kevin Hern said. Asked his favorite candidate of the three he expected to run: Vance, Rubio or DeSantis, he replied with a smile: “Everybody.”

Vance does have ardent supporters, including Sen. Jim Banks of Indiana who said before the midterms he would enthusiastically back him for president in 2028.

“If JD runs, he has my full support,” Banks said in an interview this week. “He continues to lead in all the polls on the Republican side to be the nominee. He's my friend. We come from the same part of the country, the same background, and he's what the country needs. I hope he runs. But I don't know if he's running or not.”

Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas) called Vance “a friend who I’ve had the honor to work alongside. He’s the vice president, of course he’s a front-runner.”

Rep. Riley Moore (R-W.Va.) said in an interview that it was the Republican “party” and not its “policies” that suffered massive losses last week. But he doesn’t blame Vance, and he supports him for the 2028 presidential race.

Vance, for his part, made his own allusion to the situation he’s found himself in. "I wanted to talk, of course, about the devastating loss last week. …There are a lot of people, I think, unfairly criticizing the leader of the team … a lot of staff infighting. … And of course, there's a conversation about whether the No. 2 has what it takes to ultimately lead the team.”

He finished: “I'm talking, of course, about the Ohio State Buckeyes."

item.title: Biden says he wouldn't have run in 2024 if he knew about his cancer
item.description: The former president also called his debate performance “not very consequential” in an interview with People magazine.

media:content.media:title: Former President Joe Biden speaks to a crowd during a fundraising event with the South Carolina Democratic Party at the Columbia Museum of Art on Feb. 27, 2026, in Columbia, South Carolina.

item.dc:creator: By Gregory Svirnovskiy
item.content:encoded:
Former President Joe Biden would not have run for reelection in 2024 if he had known about his cancer, he said in an interview released Wednesday in which he also sought to downplay the historic debate performance that helped end his political career.

"If I had known that I was feeling lousy because I had cancer, I would have not gone forward because I don't think an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running," he said in the interview with People magazine, which was conducted last week following Democrats’ big midterm wins and ahead of his upcoming memoir’s release.

The former president announced his diagnosis — Stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer — in May 2025, just four months after leaving the White House. It triggered an outpouring of public support — but it also raised questions about how doctors failed to catch the cancer earlier and whether it might have contributed to Biden’s apparent decline toward the end of his term.

“I think it’s very sad, actually. I’m surprised that it wasn’t, you know, the public wasn’t notified a long time ago because to get to [a Gleason score of] 9, that’s a long time,” President Donald Trump told reporters shortly after Biden’s announcement.

Prior to his diagnosis, Biden hadn’t been screened for prostate cancer since 2014. U.S. guidelines have long recommended that men shouldn't be screened for the cancer once they hit their 70s.

Biden also downplayed his poor June 2024 debate performance against Trump that contributed to his exit from the Democratic ticket a month later.

“To me, it was not very consequential,” he said. “First of all, I thought there would be another debate, which there wasn’t. But notwithstanding the fact that there wasn’t another debate, it didn’t disturb me because it wasn’t consequential.”

Biden’s son, Hunter, has said he believes the cancer was responsible for the performance. His weak showing on the debate stage led to mounting calls within his party for him to withdraw, an effort eventually backed by longtime friends and allies such as former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi.

The former president’s memoir, “Promise Me, America,” will go on sale next week. Biden wrote Sunday on X that the cancer meant he “won’t be able to do as many conversations about my book as I’d hoped.” But he still feels sharp, he told the magazine.

“I’m not saying I’ll live forever, but the point is that, you know, I have all my faculties, I have access to all the things I had before and, you know, I feel good,” he said.

item.title: Several Dem women leaned into their identity this cycle. Not in the way you think.
item.description: They focused less on the historic nature of their bids and more on parenting in a tough economy.

media:content.media:title: South Carolina Democratic Senate candidate Dr. Annie Andrews speaks during an election night event on Nov. 3, 2026, in Charleston, S.C.

item.dc:creator: By Lauren Fedor and Erin Doherty
item.dc:contributor: By Lauren Fedor and Erin Doherty
item.content:encoded:
When Annie Andrews announced her longshot campaign for U.S. Senate last May, the Democrat from South Carolina pitched herself as a “busy mom.”

“Lindsey [Graham] is going to tell you I am radical, that I am crazy,” Andrews said in her launch video. “But here’s the thing: I am literally a busy mom and a pediatrician who plays peek-a-boo with my patients, watches Bluey with my kids … and spends most of my free time shuttling them to dance, Tae Kwon Do and football.”

Now, she is one of a record number of women who will serve in the next Congress. And as a 46-year-old mother of three school-aged children, she’s among several Democratic women who flipped seats and governor’s mansions this November with campaign messages centered on parenting and affordability.

It’s a notable campaign shift from previous election cycles: This year, female candidates focused less on the historic nature of their bids, or culture war issues that have long fomented divisions over gender and electability. Instead, they zeroed in on an economic message emphasizing bread-and-butter concerns — like how rising costs were squeezing families, including theirs.

“Moms understand kitchen table issues better than perhaps anyone,” said Jessica Mackler, president of EMILY’s List, the group that recruits and backs female Democratic candidates who support abortion rights. “They understand how to stretch a paycheck. They understand what it is like to walk through a grocery store and have to put something back on the shelf.”

Senate, House and gubernatorial campaigns spent a combined $72 million on ads featuring the words “mom” or “mother” in 2026, according to AdImpact — a 50% increase from the $48 million spent in 2024 and double the spending on these kind of ads from 2022.

In many races, Democrats leaned on their experiences as parents to dismiss the kind of culture war attacks that have been effective for Republicans in recent years.

“They want to run an entire campaign saying that I’m too woke … I plan to spend an entire campaign focused on the fact that working people are too broke,” Democratic Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa said in one of her final TV ads. “My pronouns are mom, Texan and soon-to-be governor.”

Campaign messaging around gender and representation can be fraught: In 2016, Hillary Clinton’s “I’m With Her” campaign slogan fell short as she failed in her pledge to break the “highest, hardest glass ceiling.” In 2024, Kamala Harris’ campaign was decidedly less overt in its messaging about the barrier-breaking potential of her candidacy. But debates about gender seemed inescapable as Trump called her “weak” and then-Sen. JD Vance said the Democratic Party was run by “childless cat ladies.”

This cycle was different.

In a 2026 environment driven by concerns about affordability and the cost of living, Democratic operatives said it was an easy decision for women and mothers in particular to lean on their home lives to connect with voters.

At least 159 women will serve in the 120th Congress, according to the Center for American Women and Politics, with Democratic women outnumbering Republicans by roughly five-to-one. Many of the newly elected Democrats are younger moms.

Their victories, especially in battleground districts and states long seen as Republican strongholds, have emboldened Democratic groups dedicated to electing more women, who argue the candidates offer a blueprint for winning races going forward.

Veteran Democratic pollster Celinda Lake said her party’s female candidates “really got points for having the right priorities and being in touch with real people's lives."

"It used to be that women with young children just didn't run, and we were electing all these women who had grown children or no children, and then we were electing women with young children, but they were hiding them, if you will,” Lake said. “Now [candidates] were bringing them out as major credentialers, and that has been changing over time."

Winning Democratic candidates told POLITICO they did not hesitate to talk about their families and personal experiences on the trail.

“I didn’t need anyone giving me talking points on how expensive groceries are,” said Representative-elect Teresa Benitez-Thompson, who won a heavily Republican House district in northern Nevada. “I don’t need anyone telling me how expensive gas is because I am filling up my tank … running kids all around town.”

JoAnna Mendoza, a single mom who flipped a swing district in the Tucson, Arizona, suburbs – said she spent the night before the election in the emergency room with her 10-year-old son.

“That is what parents face. That is what moms go through. Their kids are sick, they have to take time off of work, or they have to leave work,” Mendoza said. “It is important for people to see themselves in their elected leaders.”

Uncomfortable questions surrounding gender and electability nevertheless persist in the run-up to the next presidential election. Some in the Democratic Party at least privately question whether they should nominate another woman at the top of the ticket in 2028.

“My message to people who would say that is: cut it out,” said Mackler. “This election clearly demonstrates that women are the drivers of Democrats' path to power, and we should embrace their leadership at all levels of the ballot.”

Lake, the Democratic pollster, said the surge in female Democratic victors showed how fed up voters are with the status quo, calling it a “Hail Mary for change.”

“It is so bad, it is so failed, we're going to elect these women who will hold people accountable,” she said, adding that voters, particularly women, “were really upset with how out of touch the older white men seemed with their families' lives” after a decade of Trump and Joe Biden running the country.

Democratic candidates do not have a monopoly on talking about family life. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, the Republican governor of Arkansas, sailed to reelection last week with a campaign that highlighted her three children and efforts to cut grocery taxes and bring down the cost of living for other families. Messages around motherhood also featured prominently at the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, earlier this year.

The messaging is part of a broader shift in the public conversation, said Abby McCloskey, a conservative policy analyst.

“For a long time, to be taken seriously in politics, your professional side went first and your personal side went far after, and that was especially the case for women,” she said. “I think there's been broader cultural shifts that, and probably in a desire for authenticity and connection, why that is no longer necessarily the case.”Democratic campaign veterans said the renewed focus on motherhood gave their candidates an edge as they try to counter swing voters’ deep-seated biases against female candidates.

One Democratic pollster, granted anonymity to speak candidly about voters’ biases, said voters still have “bad reactions” to women running for office who are perceived as “cold.” Talking about motherhood and family life, the pollster said, allowed candidates to come across as warm while pushing back against the idea that their candidates are too radical or left-wing.

“In some of these places where you have to win over a bunch of conservative folks, the candidate can come across as just a regular mom,” the pollster said. “Not a scary, left, woke lady.”

The beginning of Jocelyn Benson’s campaign launch video showed the Democrat hugging her son in their family’s kitchen. Now Michigan’s Democratic governor-elect, Benson told POLITICO she was “very intentional” about inviting kids to join her on stage during her celebration on Election Night.

“I think leaders in this moment, and I think parents, moms in particular, recognize this as an opportunity to show a different way of leading and of being a good person and a good citizen,” she said.

item.title: Wes Moore wants immigration reform. Can he work with Stephen Miller?
item.description: The possible 2028 contender told POLITICO that Democrats should try to work with the president’s new chief of staff despite a “well of distrust.”

media:content.media:description: Gov. Wes Moore on Stephen Miller: ‘I will work with anybody, I will bow to nobody’
media:content.media:title: Gov. Wes Moore on Stephen Miller: ‘I will work with anybody, I will bow to nobody’

item.dc:creator: By Aaron Pellish
item.content:encoded:
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore said Democrats should work toward bipartisan deals, including on immigration, with Stephen Miller — despite the “well of distrust” he holds for the new White House chief of staff.

Moore, a potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidate, told POLITICO’s Alex Burns on Tuesday that even though Miller is “the architect of some of the most racist, xenophobic, homophobic policies that we have,” he still believes there’s room to negotiate with the White House to ease the targeting of unauthorized immigrants living in the U.S.

“One thing I've always said to the people of my state is I will work with anybody, I will bow to nobody,” he said at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce’s B20 Summit.

“I wish that there was a different team, because I think the well of distrust that Stephen Miller and his policies have fostered have been deeply poisonous,” the governor continued. “But I still want to make sure that we're doing good things on behalf of the people of our jurisdictions, and I do think we have a window to do it.”

President Donald Trump floated the possibility of a bipartisan immigration deal during a “60 Minutes” interview on Sunday as he acknowledged that the aggressive deportation policies he enacted at the beginning of his term were “too tough” and “took people that had good jobs.” Trump appeared to reverse course on Monday, telling reporters he opposed offering “amnesty” for undocumented immigrants.

Voters have long said Trump’s mass deportation campaign is too aggressive, and some Hill Republicans have pointed the blame at Miller, who masterminded the policy, for their lost support among Hispanics this midterm cycle. Moore said there’s a window for “real bipartisan agreement” on immigration despite Miller’s ascension last week.

Oklahoma GOP Gov. Kevin Stitt, who co-chairs the National Governors Association with Moore and also spoke at the summit, said Trump “won on a strong border” — but governors need a “seat at the table” when it comes to issuing workforce permits.

Asked what message it sends to international business to have a top staffer in the White House who is a hardliner on immigration, Stitt deflected.

“I'm not going to speak to his hardlineness on that issue,” Stitt said, referring to Miller. He added that he thinks there’s a path forward for unauthorized immigrants contributing to the economy: “If you are here chasing the American dream, contributing to society, and you've come here illegally and a company is vouching for you, that's literally what we want. We educate people here, we want the best and brightest here, and I think there's a solution.”

Stitt, who has not spoken to Trump since the midterms, said the president has "softened" on immigration in recent interviews.

“There's a real solution, and I think President Trump can lead on it. He can lead and hopefully ... the Democrat majority in the House and the Senate will now work with him and we can get something done,” the Republican governor said.

Moore, in the interview, also pointed to AI safety as an area for potential bipartisan agreement and urged the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress to create federal regulations on AI companies that include “protections on our pocketbooks” along with protections for workforce development and infrastructure.

So far, much of the regulation has been left to the states. But Democrats in Congress are weighing multiple bills to enact safety standards protecting consumers from AI as Americans grow increasingly concernedabout the dangers of the technology.

“It’s not useful to have 50 different guidelines for how this country should think about this,” Moore said. “We need Washington to get in the game.”

The Democrat also warned businesses to stay away from Trump’s ballroom and meme coin.

"I would tell you right now that this will not age well,” Moore told the audience at the B20 summit. “There will not be a long term benefit to this. That with the American people, the best way for us to fight for capitalism is to make sure that we're building a system that everyone can see the benefit for and that we're not parsing off who it can actually benefit."

Andrew Howard contributed to this report.

item.title: Democrats plot their course on national popular vote
item.description: Democrats have won unified control of enough swing states — Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, and Michigan — to sidestep the Electoral College. Will they back the effort?

media:content.media:title: Pennsylvania Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gov. Josh Shapiro meets with constituents at a Pittsburgh Steelers watch party at the Cork Harbour Pub on October 25, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Incumbent Shapiro is leading Republican candidate Stacy Garrity in fundraising and recent polling.

item.dc:creator: By Aaron Pellish and Lisa Kashinsky
item.dc:contributor: By Aaron Pellish and Lisa Kashinsky
item.content:encoded:
Democrats who just triumphed in a number of battlegrounds are facing pressure to make their states just a little less powerful in the fight for the presidency.

The party’s sweeping victories present an opportunity for Democrats in states with newly won trifectas to join the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement between states to make sure whoever wins national popular vote becomes president by awarding their Electoral College votes to that winner, rather than the winner of the most votes in their state.

The compact would go into effect when it’s enacted in states whose combined electoral vote total is at least 270. Currently, 18 historically blue states and Washington D.C. have joined the compact, a two-decade-long, nonpartisan project, with a combined 222 electoral votes.

That means if Pennsylvania, Michigan and Wisconsin join, along with either Arizona or Nevada, the compact would go into effect in every member state, making it possible for the next president to be elected by winning the popular vote while losing the Electoral College. All five states will now be under unified Democratic control starting next year.

Democrats in those five states, which will likely be battlegrounds in 2028 under the current system, have supported switching to national popular vote in the past.

But it’s unclear whether they will move forward on national popular vote after gaining historic trifectas on the back of promising to lower costs for voters — a move that would make their own states less crucial for the 2028 presidential battle.

Incoming Arizona Senate Majority Leader Priya Sundareshan told POLITICO her caucus will take up the national popular vote, but the timing remains unsettled. Sundareshan added she hasn’t spoken to Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs about national popular vote. Hobbs’ office declined to comment.

“We certainly are and have been prepared to join the compact, and we also want to make sure that we are showing that our priorities are reflective of what we really focused on on the campaign trail,” she said.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro told POLITICO he is “open” to signing his state into the compact but suggested he hasn’t yet coordinated with state legislators on how national popular vote fits in with the rest of his agenda. He said separately Saturday at Crooked Media’s “Crooked Con” that the national popular vote “makes sense” and pledged to work with lawmakers “to figure out what the right mechanism going forward on that.”

Some state leaders say they know they’d draw challenges and political fury if they attempt to rewrite the nation’s rules for electing presidents. Incoming Michigan Senate Majority Leader Darrin Camilleri said he’s open to enacting a national popular vote, but conceded that any change would likely invite lawsuits from Republicans.

“Other states that have done this are not going to be the tipping-point states. We very well could be one of those tipping point-states, and so I want to ensure that everybody is on the same page,” Camilleri said.

Michigan Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson’s representatives did not respond to a request for comment.

Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley previously backed a 2019 bill to have Wisconsin join the compact. When asked if he would do so as governor, Crowley said in a statement he “is focused on assembling an experienced transition team so his administration can be ready on day one to deliver results for working families across the Badger State.”

Ben Wikler, the former Wisconsin Democratic Party chair and national popular vote advocate, dismissed concerns about battleground states diminishing their prominence in presidential elections, even as he acknowledged that “battleground states passing the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact is like the popular kids abolishing the concept of popularity.”

“I've spoken to audiences all over the state of Wisconsin,” Wikler said. “Everyone here agrees that Wisconsinites shouldn't be high and mighty, lording over the powerless voters in the coastal states. We should be a one-person, one-vote democracy.”

When Nevada Democrats held a trifecta in 2019, they put a bill to join the compact on former Gov. Steve Sisolak’s desk, but Sisolak vetoed it out of concern it would diminish the role of smaller states like Nevada in the electoral process. Nevada Gov.-elect Aaron Ford’s office declined to comment.

Despite the uncertainty, the outside groups pushing the compact are optimistic enough states will join to trigger the compact ahead of the 2028 election.

“I’ve never been more confident in my life,” said Patrick Rosenstiel, a spokesperson for National Popular Vote, the bipartisan group behind the compact.

item.title: A new set of Democratic power brokers just dropped before 2028
item.description: Presidential hopefuls are already working the phones to build relationships with the new slate of Democratic figures in key early states.

media:content.media:title: Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) stands with newly elected Democratic senators in his office suite at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, on Nov. 9, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Lisa Kashinsky, Alec Hernandez and Erin Doherty
item.dc:contributor: By Lisa Kashinsky, Alec Hernandez and Erin Doherty
item.content:encoded:
The 2028 presidential race is already playing out in the text threads and phone calls of a new set of Democratic power brokers.

A number of would-be White House contenders — including former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, former Ambassador Rahm Emanuel and Sens. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) and Cory Booker (D-N.J.) — have already reached out to various winners, interviews with rumored 2028 hopefuls and newly elected Democrats reveal.

Incoming Reps. Nancy Lacore (D-S.C.) and Teresa Benitez-Thompson (D-Nev.), incoming Sens. Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, Chris Pappas in New Hampshire and Annie Andrews in South Carolina, and New Mexico Gov.-elect Deb Haaland all got calls.

The outreach signals a desire among Democrats who surfed a massive blue wave to victory last week to leverage those wins and influence the coming presidential contest, both in key early primary states and battlegrounds.

"Lots of congratulatory calls with 'we would like to have conversations soon,'" said Morgan Jackson, a senior adviser to Sen.-elect Roy Cooper in North Carolina.

Some newly elected Democrats are openly positioning themselves as kingmakers on the road to 2028, arguing their campaigns offer templates for the next crop of White House aspirants. Others are positioning themselves as ambassadors to their states.

El-Sayed wants his party's next presidential nominee to support passing progressive policies like Medicare for All — and told POLITICO he hopes they’ll agree with his unflinching criticism of U.S. military support for Israel. Incoming Michigan Rep. William Lawrence said that Democrats won a “clear mandate” to take on Big Tech, including data centers, and to prevent endless wars, and he wants those issues to stay on “top of the agenda for 2028.” Haaland told POLITICO ahead of Election Day she wants Democrats to "have a plan for Indian tribes."

Their rise will influence the potential 2028 field’s ability to navigate new geography and new demands while courting established kingmakers and party leaders. And some warning signs are already emerging: Allies of Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa's are knives out for Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who they argue didn't do enough to help her as chair of the Democratic Governors Association and doesn't understand the power of Latino voters — a necessary component of any 2028 bid.

First stop: South Carolina

No state will be as central as South Carolina, which will go first on Democrats' presidential primary calendar and where the bench of candidates will be deepest.

Longtime Democratic Rep. Jim Clyburn (S.C.) is still expected to reprise his role as the host and kingmaker. But Andrews’ and Lacore’s massive upsets last Tuesday have supercharged Democrats’ delegation in the state.

Andrews has fielded multiple calls from potential presidential candidates since Election Day, according to a person with direct knowledge of her conversations. Lacore, too, has taken “many” congratulatory calls from potential Democratic candidates, per another person with direct knowledge. Sens. Raphael Warnock of Georgia and Kelly both campaigned for Andrews during the race, and Buttigieg and Beshear made appearances with Lacore in her coastal district.

Clyburn has long been vocal about the direction of the Democratic Party, active on the trail and open with his endorsements and advice to presidential hopefuls — and just recently with POLITICO. It’s not clear how the two newcomers will seek to shape 2028: Representatives for both campaigns declined to comment.

But Andrews, a pediatrician, made health care a central part of her campaign. And Lacore’s focus on veterans’ issues and national security could bring those to the forefront. The two of them and Clyburn are set to meet on Capitol Hill for the first time as South Carolina’s incoming delegation on Wednesday to plan how best to work together in Congress, according to a person familiar with the gathering.

Antjuan Seawright, a Clyburn adviser and Democratic strategist, said the three Palmetto State Democrats will likely have “different” approaches to their involvement in the 2028 primary.

“The three of them, individually and collectively, will have a tremendous opportunity to entertain and introduce South Carolina to the potential candidates who are seeking the office,” Seawright said.

Kicking the tires in New Hampshire

New Hampshire’s elected Democrats have long wielded outsize influence over the party’s nominating process in what was the first-in-the-nation primary state. Pappas, a four-term representative, and Rep.-elect Stefany Shaheen, the daughter of two longtime New Hampshire Democratic power players, are well steeped in 2028 after multiple potential candidates campaigned with them through the fall to gain footholds in the state.

Pappas started signaling his status as a power broker in the final days of the election, and was on Kelly’s list of election-night phone calls.

“We had a lot of visitors at the end of this campaign, maybe some folks who were just using me as an excuse to come visit New Hampshire and kick the tires a little bit,” Pappas said on WMUR in a post-election interview.

Pappas told POLITICO on Monday he would “certainly” serve as an ambassador for candidates — and suggested there are “people who want to certainly come back soon. I think it’s going to kick off pretty quickly.”

Jim Demers, a veteran Democratic strategist and liaison for presidential hopefuls in the state, told POLITICO he believes both Pappas and Shaheen could serve as key conduits for candidates looking to play in New Hampshire.

“Both of them are very campaign smart, and so their advice to any of the potential presidential candidates will be important,” Demers said. “I would expect they’re going to be extremely popular and can be a big help to any of them who want help.”

The progressive agenda in Michigan

Michigan is already the epicenter of the Democratic Party’s most polarizing fights over policy and ideology. Now, the perennial battleground sits fifth in the presidential primary lineup.

Few have been so openly positioning themselves to join the ranks of the state’s power brokers as El-Sayed, who declared even before his primary win that he would “dog” presidential hopefuls “up and down the state” to embrace his progressive platform, including Medicare for All.

“It’s important to me that I've got a governing partner,” El-Sayed told POLITICO in a post-election interview. “I'm going to do what I can to make sure that I get one.”

El-Sayed could play a significant role in shaping the debate over Israel in a state that gave rise to the “uncommitted” movement in 2024 — and where he ran aggressively against U.S. military aid to the country.

The senator-elect said he hopes the next nominee will share his stance; when asked about that remark, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said he looks forward to “having a thoughtful conversation with” El-Sayed on the topic.

“I will be advocating for what I believe to be right, and clearly my state agrees with me on this issue,” El-Sayed said, adding, “If you want to be where the voters are — if you want to be on the side of peace and on the side of justice and transparency — I believe that that is around holding Israel accountable to its war crimes and on making sure our tax dollars get used to do good things here rather than bad things somewhere else.”

Others are ready to engage with their party’s future in a more neutral role. Jocelyn Benson, the moderate incoming governor, said in an interview that she will “certainly invite folks to come to our state to make their case to our residents.”

Over in the West

The West will have its biggest role in the calendar yet, with New Mexico joining Nevada as early calendar stops.

As Nevada’s new top official with strong working-class appeal, Democratic Gov.-elect Aaron Ford could play a major role in shepherding 2028 candidates — should he choose to. He’s already fielded congratulatory calls from Moore, who leads the National Governors Association, and others.

Benitez-Thompson, who will represent the large swath of rural northern Nevada, is already embracing her role as an ambassador for the region and has taken calls from a “number” of likely presidential contenders in the days after the midterm election.

“I am dead set on making sure that I can bring resources home for northern Nevada and investments home into northern Nevada. I'll be talking to any and everyone who can help me move resources and levers to make that happen,” she said in an interview. "Come to northern Nevada, step off of the plane, but be ready for me to show you what our needs are."

Adam Wren, Ali Bianco, Lauren Fedor, Aaron Pellish and Meredith Lee Hill contributed to this report.

item.title: Court filing alleges Trump adviser received cash, luxury gifts from foreign interests
item.description: The filing from Alex Bruesewitz’s ex-business partner Derek Utley is a response to an earlier lawsuit claiming Utley embezzled millions from their firm, X Strategies.

media:content.media:title: Alex Bruesewitz during the Trump Accounts Launch Summit in Washington, on an. 28, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Jason Beeferman
item.content:encoded:
A former business partner is accusing MAGA media guru Alex Bruesewitz of receiving lavish gifts from foreign individuals in Qatar and Syria while also pursuing lucrative deals with other entities looking to unlock access to U.S. government officials.

The allegations were made in a court filing Monday by Derek Utley, who co-founded the digital firm X Strategies in 2017 with Bruesewitz. Bruesewitz is a top outside adviser to President Donald Trump, having helped shape his 2024 campaign’s digital strategy, and X Strategies maintains the Trump War Room and Team Trump accounts on X.

The company sued Utley in September, alleging he embezzled and gambled away millions of dollars from the firm.

In the Monday filing responding to that lawsuit, Utley calls it a “marketing ploy masquerading as a federal lawsuit” and denies allegations he embezzled the company’s money or used its funds to gamble. The filing includes a countersuit against X Strategies that claims Utley was fired from the company without cause over a requested medical leave. (The firm’s original lawsuit had claimed Utley submitted “fake medical records” to "fraudulently" get six months paid leave, and was then fired.)

Utley doesn’t explicitly accuse Bruesewitz of offering foreign officials political access in exchange for payments, but charges that Bruesewitz “pursued substantial business and financial relationships with foreign individuals, investors, and governmental representatives, including persons associated with Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, and Syria” while concealing those relationships. The filing does not include documentation to support its allegations.

“The relationships and access Bruesewitz cultivated through X Strategies were valuable commercial assets, particularly to foreign interests seeking introductions to American political figures, access to governmental institutions, or assistance advancing their commercial and political objectives,” the filing says. “Upon information and belief, Bruesewitz received approximately $500,000 from individuals associated with Qatar in connection with an undisclosed business or consulting arrangement.”

Bruesewitz’s lawyer Bradford Cohen denied all the allegations.

“These are things that would be defamatory if made outside the four corners of the complaint,” Cohen said Monday evening, vowing to "vigorously" defend against the allegations.

“We're asserting that everything in his factual allegations is either untrue, exaggerated, or completely fabricated,” he said. “Desperate men resort to desperate things, and this screams of desperation.”

Bruesewitz continues to advise conservative figures in Trump’s orbit. He also leveraged his relationships with foreign officials when the war with Iran broke out to help charter a flight back to the U.S. for himself and other Americans who were stranded in Qatar, according to his social media posts at the time.

Utley did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Neither did the White House.

In another example, Utley claims Bruesewitz sought to charge an annual advisory fee of $1 million to a “Copenhagen-based investment firm with holdings in the United States and Europe.” The proposed deal, the filing said, included services like “providing access to American governmental officials, federal agencies, and financial institutions.”

“These circumstances raise questions concerning potential registration and disclosure obligations under FARA,” the court filing says, referencing the Foreign Agents Registration Act, which requires public disclosures from those involved in lobbying or other activities representing foreign interests.

Additionally, the filing alleges that Bruesewitz told Utley that his honeymoon hotel stay in the Maldives was paid for by “two Syrian billionaires” who provided access to a suite that ordinarily costs $15,000 a night.

Bruesewitz has previously advocated for conservative influencers to disclose their relationships with foreign governments seeking to sway the Trump administration. He also said during a June interview with Tucker Carlson that he does not take any foreign payments.

“Getting foreign influence out of the political ecosystem, specifically online, is a very — it’s a passion project of mine,” Bruesewitz said in the interview. “You can only imagine the type of money that these countries and other companies have tried to throw at me. I do not take any foreign money. I don’t take any money from the Gulf countries. I don't take any money from India. I don't take any money from Russia, China. No foreign countries.”

item.title: Josh Shapiro says Texas won’t replace Pennsylvania as the ‘ultimate swing state’
item.description: The governor romped to a 22-point reelection victory last week.

media:content.media:title: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro speaks at an election night event on Nov. 3, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Lisa Kashinsky
item.content:encoded:
Democrats’ blue wave blew up the 2028 battle map. But Josh Shapiro insists Texas isn’t going to replace Pennsylvania as the “ultimate swing state.”

He needs it to be true.

Shapiro’s theory of the case for 2028 has long rested on his ability to win resoundingly and repeatedly in what has recently been the nation’s biggest battleground state. On Tuesday, he helped deliver Democrats four congressional flips and their first trifecta in Harrisburg in three decades, all while running up a more than 20-point margin in his own reelection bid. He plowed over $10 million into state Democrats’ campaign arms and helped recruit and cut ads for candidates across House and state Senate races. He also flipped 11 counties President Donald Trump won in 2024 and, his team argued in a post-election memo shared first with POLITICO, showed “unique strength” with voters skeptical of the Democratic Party.

It’s a significant show of force even in a wave election — one that could springboard him into a presidential bid if he chooses, even as Democrats turn their attention to redder turf.

“The common-sense approach we’ve taken to governing, the kind of candidates we recruited to run for Congress who won, I think that that can be a model for our party,” Shapiro told POLITICO by phone late last week. And “it’s going to be important that we share our Pennsylvania model from what I would maintain … is still the ultimate swing state.”

Shapiro continues to play coy about his presidential ambitions. He phoned Democrats’ primary kingmaker, Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-S.C.), after the election, but declined to discuss the details. When POLITICO asked Shapiro his timeline to decide a 2028 run, he replied: “I just wrapped up a meeting with the legislative leaders and my senior team to work on our agenda going forward, and that's what I'm focused on right now.”

Here’s more from POLITICO’s chat with Shapiro, edited and condensed for length.

You’ve got your trifecta. What’s your No. 1 priority?

The first bill that will reach my desk will be to raise the minimum wage to 15 bucks an hour. I've been able to get a lot of stuff done through the Republican Legislature, but that's an example of something that hasn't.

Is signing onto the National Popular Vote Compact something you’d be interested in?

I have said that I am open to that, I think I’ve voiced some positivity toward it. As it relates to the trifecta, though, the leaders and I agreed that we would speak with one voice in announcing our initial agenda.

A lot of Democrats are saying the biggest message that they got out of this wave election was the economy. Do you think that that's the biggest takeaway?

I think in part that is correct, and that's why the first new law I want to pass in Pennsylvania is to put more money in people's pockets. I also think there was something deeper. … Substantively the issue that obviously mattered most was the high cost of everything; I think underneath that was a real fear that people had about the direction this country was going in, and they wanted to use their power to change it.

Do you think the path to the presidency is moving out of the Blue Wall and into states like Texas, into the Sun Belt?

Democrats are proving that we can win everywhere. … We added back to the Blue Wall. Ohio, with Amy [Acton]'s incredible victory there. I was proud to campaign for her.

We’re showing we can win in these southern states. So I think the takeaway from Tuesday night is the map got a whole lot bigger for Democrats. And so long as Republicans continue to follow Trump and [Vice President JD] Vance off the cliff, their map is getting much smaller.

Do you think that Texas will take over from Pennsylvania as the nation's biggest swing state?

I mean, they're a big state, and they were just won by two outstanding Democrats. I was so impressed with both of them and how they ran their campaigns. And I imagine Texas is going to have a lot to say about the future leadership in our country.

But not necessarily taking over Pennsylvania’s spot —

I mean, come on. I’m Pennsylvania first. You’re never going to get me to come off of Pennsylvania being the ultimate swing state.

Abdul El-Sayed told me he hopes the next Democratic presidential nominee shares his views on Israel. He opposes military aid to Israel. Do you agree that that's the stance the nominee, whoever it is, should take?

Well, he is one voice in our party. And I look forward to getting a chance to talk to him and learn more about how he really thinks and how he really views these issues, and having a thoughtful conversation with him.

Is there anyone coming out of Tuesday who you want to talk to, who you think ‘that person has a good message for the party’?

I've talked to probably more than 20 people across the country since Tuesday night who won races at all levels. I've been incredibly impressed by the talent that chose to run for office and won in really tough states. I think I can learn from a lot of them, and I want to learn from them, and I want to listen to them, and I salute their victories.
